chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The NVIDIA Inflection

On December 18, 2024, Navitas Semiconductor announced that it was working with NVIDIA on next-generation 800-volt high-voltage direct-current power architecture for AI data centre deployments. The company's shares approximately doubled intraday — the single largest re-rating event in Navitas's post-SPAC history — condensing into a single trading session a thesis that management had been building since the 2014 founding in Torrance, California.

Navitas (NVTS: NASDAQ) is the principal SPAC-listed pure-play in gallium nitride and silicon carbide wide-bandgap power semiconductors. Its co-founders, Gene Sheridan and Dan Kinzer, spent the better part of their careers at International Rectifier — one of the heritage power semiconductor companies that Infineon Technologies absorbed for roughly $3 billion in January 2015 — before striking out to build around GaNFast, a monolithic integrated GaN power IC that packages driver, protection, and logic onto a single die. The October 2021 SPAC merger with Live Oak Acquisition Corp II valued the company at approximately $1 billion. An August 2022 acquisition of GeneSiC Semiconductor for roughly $215 million in stock added a silicon carbide device portfolio and, critically, GeneSiC founder Ranbir Singh's SiC engineering team.

## Financial Baseline and the Navitas 2.0 Reset

The revenue trajectory tells the story of a company mid-pivot:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD M) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 | $23.7 | SPAC listing year |
| 2022 | $37.9 | GeneSiC year |
| 2023 | $93.0 | Mobile fast-charger peak |
| 2024 | $83.3 | Contraction begins |
| 2025 | $45.9 | Navitas 2.0 restructuring |
| Q1 2026 | $8.6 (+18% seq.) | Floor declared at $7.3M in Q4 2025 |

The compression from $93 million to $45.9 million was deliberate. Navitas 2.0 shed the lower-margin mobile fast-charger distribution channels that had supplied Xiaomi, OPPO, Vivo and OnePlus OEMs in China, redirecting engineering and commercial resources toward AI data centre power, grid infrastructure, and industrial electrification. A Q4 2025 private placement raised $95.6 million, leaving the company with $236.9 million in cash and zero debt — roughly four years of runway at the prevailing operating burn rate. By Q1 2026, cash had drawn down to $221 million as restructuring costs continued to run through the income statement.

The strategic logic is visible in the Q1 2026 mix: high-power business grew 35 percent year-on-year and, for the first time, exceeded mobile revenue as a share of total. AI infrastructure revenue specifically grew 50 percent sequentially from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026. The non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 39.0 percent, compared with 38.7 percent in Q4 2025. The company guided Q2 2026 revenue to approximately $10 million, implying roughly 16 percent sequential growth. The path to profitability remains distant, but the trajectory at the segment level began to inflect in Q1.

## The NVIDIA Architecture Partnership

The formal public disclosure came on [May 21, 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/05/21/3086170/0/en/NVIDIA-Selects-Navitas-to-Collaborate-on-Next-Generation-800-V-HVDC-Architecture.html), when NVIDIA selected Navitas to collaborate on its 800V HVDC architecture for "Kyber" rack-scale systems powering Rubin Ultra GPUs. The architecture promises a five percent improvement in end-to-end power efficiency, a 70 percent reduction in power-supply maintenance costs relative to legacy 54-volt topologies, and materially lower cooling expense by taking high-voltage direct current directly to the IT rack. Navitas's contribution spans the full power chain — grid to GPU — combining GaNSafe power ICs with integrated short-circuit protection and programmable slew-rate control alongside GeneSiC trench-assisted planar SiC MOSFETs for the higher-voltage stages.

Sheridan, still CEO at the time, was direct:

> "We are proud to support NVIDIA's 800 HVDC architecture initiative. Our latest innovations in high-power GaN and SiC technologies have seen world firsts and have created new inflections into markets such as AI datacenters and electric vehicles. With our broad portfolio range, we're able to support NVIDIA's 800V HVDC infrastructure, from grid to the GPU."

Engineering samples shipped in Q4 2025; [supplier selections were targeted for 2026](https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/05/05/live-navitas-semiconductor-q1-earnings-tonight-can-the-676-surge-survive-the-print/). In March 2026, Navitas debuted a 20 kW 800V-to-6V DC-DC power delivery board at NVIDIA GTC, the first tangible hardware demonstration of the collaboration.

## GlobalFoundries and the US Manufacturing Bet

On [November 20, 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/11/20/3191921/0/en/GlobalFoundries-and-Navitas-Semiconductor-Partner-to-Accelerate-U-S-GaN-Technology-and-Manufacturing-for-AI-Datacenters-and-Critical-Power-Applications.html), Navitas and GlobalFoundries announced a long-term strategic manufacturing partnership targeting US-based GaN production at GF's Burlington, Vermont facility — a site with established high-voltage GaN-on-silicon capability. Development work began in early 2026 with production targeted for the second half of 2026; Navitas has outlined an eight-inch wafer transition for GaN by 2027. The partnership addresses both supply-chain resilience under the CHIPS and Science Act framework and the domestic-sourcing requirements that large hyperscaler customers are beginning to impose.

> "GaN adoption is accelerating in high power semiconductor markets," Allexandre said at the announcement. "Our collaboration with GF ensures we can deliver the performance and scale our customers demand."

## Allexandre Takes the Helm

Gene Sheridan stepped down as chief executive on August 31, 2025, handing operational control to Chris Allexandre on September 1. Allexandre came from Renesas Electronics, where as SVP and general manager of the power division he ran a roughly $2.5 billion business that had itself been repositioned toward cloud infrastructure, automotive, and industrial markets. Kinzer, the technical co-founder, remained as COO and CTO, anchoring engineering continuity. Q1 2026 was effectively Allexandre's first full reported quarter as chief executive, and he framed it explicitly as validation:

> "Q1 was the first clear proof point, and the growth in high power market demonstrate the momentum of our Navitas 2.0 strategy."

His strategic scope was unambiguous at the Q1 2026 earnings call: "We are singularly focused on four high-growth, high-value market segments: AI data center, energy and green infrastructure, performance computing, and industrial electrification." He cited a serviceable addressable market of $3.5 billion by 2030 across those segments, with a combined CAGR he put above 60 percent.

## The Open Questions

The dossier's forward work centres on three unresolved vectors. First, whether Allexandre can translate the Navitas 2.0 restructuring into sustained revenue acceleration: Q2 2026 guidance of $10 million is a directionally positive signal, but the company remains pre-profit and the mobile revenue base has not yet been replaced in absolute terms. Second, what the NVIDIA 800V partnership actually delivers in revenue — supplier selections and ramp timing for Rubin Ultra / Kyber remain the critical near-term milestones. Third, Navitas competes in GaN against Infineon CoolGaN and Power Integrations' InnoMux GaN, and in SiC against Wolfspeed, ON Semiconductor, STMicroelectronics, and Infineon's Kulim SiC expansion — all better-capitalised and with deeper existing customer relationships. The Burlington manufacturing buildout, if executed on schedule, addresses the US-sourcing requirement and provides a differentiated supply-chain story; whether that story translates to pricing power and design wins remains the central empirical question.

---

chapters.title: From 2014 Torrance founding through SPAC, GeneSiC, NVIDIA, and Allexandre
chapters.body:
## The Garage Before the Gallium

When Gene Sheridan and Dan Kinzer left International Rectifier in 2014, they carried with them a combined half-century of power-semiconductor muscle memory — and a conviction that the industry's foundational material, silicon, was running out of room. Sheridan had spent more than two decades at the El Segundo-based power IC house, rising to Senior Vice President of Worldwide Sales and Marketing. Kinzer had anchored its engineering organisation through successive product generations. Together, in Torrance, California — a few miles from their old employer — they founded Navitas Semiconductor with the explicit thesis that gallium nitride would displace silicon in the next wave of power conversion.

The timing carried irony. Less than four months after Navitas was incorporated, Infineon Technologies completed its acquisition of International Rectifier for approximately $3 billion in January 2015, absorbing the institution that had shaped both founders. The deal was a bookmark on an era. Sheridan and Kinzer were already building what came next.

The technology they pursued was monolithic integration — embedding GaN transistors and their gate-drive, protection, and sensing circuitry on a single die, rather than the hybrid multi-chip approaches that had characterised earlier GaN experimentation. The result was GaNFast, Navitas's flagship power IC platform, which promised switching speeds five to fifty times faster than silicon counterparts at materially higher efficiency. Kinzer, as Chief Operating Officer and Chief Technology Officer, anchored the engineering programme. Sheridan managed the strategic and commercial architecture. The company kept a deliberately small footprint through the second half of the decade, refining the platform and building a design-win pipeline before demanding volume production.

## Fast Chargers and the SPAC Window

The commercial breakthrough came from an unexpected application: the smartphone charger. As handset makers in China raced to offer ever-higher wattages — 65W, 100W, then beyond — the conventional silicon charger brick became the constraint. GaNFast ICs enabled chargers that were smaller, cooler, and more efficient at the same power level. Between 2020 and 2022, Navitas built design-win momentum across the major Chinese OEMs: Xiaomi, OPPO, Vivo, and OnePlus all deployed GaNFast-based chargers, giving the company its first meaningful revenue ramp. Navitas revenue grew from $23.7 million in 2021 to $37.9 million in 2022, then surged to $93.0 million in 2023 as the mobile fast-charger channel scaled.

Against that commercial backdrop, Navitas executed its public listing. On October 19, 2021, the company completed a SPAC merger with Live Oak Acquisition Corp II at an enterprise value of approximately $1 billion, listing on NASDAQ under the ticker NVTS. The SPAC structure, then near the peak of its post-pandemic vogue, offered Navitas a faster route to the public markets than a conventional IPO process would have allowed, and the enterprise value reflected both the GaNFast commercial traction and the broader investor appetite for wide-bandgap power semiconductor exposure. Richard Hendrix, associated with the Live Oak vehicle, joined the Navitas board as part of the combination and remained a director thereafter.

## The GeneSiC Acquisition

The mobile fast-charger market, however useful as a proof-of-concept for GaN, was never the addressable market that would justify a billion-dollar valuation. The larger prize — electric-vehicle on-board chargers, solar inverters, industrial motor drives, and eventually data-centre power supplies — required silicon carbide as well as gallium nitride. SiC devices handle the highest voltage and current levels in the power conversion stack, complementing GaN's dominance at intermediate power densities.

In August 2022, Navitas acquired GeneSiC Semiconductor for approximately $215 million in stock. GeneSiC was a small, engineering-heavy SiC power device company whose founder, Ranbir Singh, had built a portfolio of SiC JFETs, Schottky diodes, and MOSFETs that complemented the GaNFast product line without cannibalising it. The acquisition was explicitly a technology and talent transaction. Singh joined the Navitas leadership structure, and the GeneSiC engineering team was integrated into what became a two-platform product portfolio: GaN for fast-charger, solar microinverter, and mid-power applications; SiC for traction, industrial, and high-voltage conversion.

The combined portfolio allowed Navitas to pitch itself as the pure-play wide-bandgap house — the only publicly listed company whose entire product line resided in next-generation semiconductor materials, with neither the legacy silicon business nor the fabrication-asset overhead of the integrated device manufacturers against whom it competed. That positioning would prove consequential when the data-centre power market began its AI-driven inflection.

## The NVIDIA Announcement

On December 18, 2024, Navitas issued a press release that rewrote its market capitalisation in a single session. The company disclosed a strategic partnership with NVIDIA to develop power architectures for NVIDIA's next-generation artificial intelligence data-centre infrastructure — specifically, an 800-volt high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) power distribution system designed to feed the extreme power densities of GPU clusters at hyperscale facilities.

The logic was technical and economic simultaneously. Conventional 48V data-centre power buses require heavy copper interconnects and multi-stage conversion to reach the point-of-load voltages that server ASICs demand. Moving the distribution bus to 800V reduces conduction losses and copper weight at scale — but requires power semiconductors that can switch efficiently at those voltages. GaN and SiC, operating comfortably above silicon's practical limits, were the natural material set. The NVIDIA partnership positioned Navitas not merely as a component supplier but as an architecture co-developer in what the company described as the defining power-infrastructure transition for the AI era.

Markets reacted with unusual conviction. NVTS shares rose approximately 150 percent on the announcement date, a re-rating that no single quarterly earnings report had produced in the company's post-SPAC history. The move reflected both the strategic credibility NVIDIA's imprimatur conferred and the scale of the addressable opportunity: hyperscale data-centre capital expenditure was running at hundreds of billions of dollars annually, and the power-delivery stack represented a material fraction of that figure.

| Revenue Period | USD (M) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 23.7 | Pre-SPAC year of listing |
| 2022 | 37.9 | GeneSiC acquired August |
| 2023 | 93.0 | Mobile fast-charger peak |
| 2024 | 83.3 | Navitas 2.0 transition begins |
| 2025 | 45.9 | Deliberate channel shedding |
| Q1 2026 | 8.6 | Sequential floor recovery; high-power >mobile |

## Navitas 2.0 and the Allexandre Succession

The NVIDIA partnership catalysed a strategic reckoning. The mobile fast-charger distribution channels that had funded Navitas through its early commercial years were lower-margin, commoditising, and inconsistent with the company's repositioning toward AI data-centre power. Beginning in 2024 and accelerating through 2025, management deliberately shed those channels — accepting a sharp revenue compression from $83.3 million in 2024 to $45.9 million in 2025 — in exchange for a cleaner, higher-margin business mix oriented toward what it branded Navitas 2.0.

The restructuring coincided with a leadership transition that had the character of a planned succession. Gene Sheridan stepped down as Chief Executive Officer on August 31, 2025, after eleven years leading the company he co-founded. On September 1, 2025, Chris Allexandre assumed the role. Allexandre came from Renesas Electronics, where he had served as Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Power Division — a business of approximately $2.5 billion in annual revenue — bringing the large-scale semiconductor operating experience that Navitas required for its next phase. Dan Kinzer, the co-founder, remained as Chief Operating Officer and Chief Technology Officer, providing engineering continuity from the GaNFast origin through the AI data-centre pivot.

The capital structure was shored up to match the ambition. In the fourth quarter of 2025, Navitas completed a $95.6 million private placement, bringing its cash position to approximately $236.9 million and extending its runway well into the commercial scaling period for its NVIDIA-aligned product roadmap. In late 2025 the company also announced a strategic manufacturing partnership with GlobalFoundries for US-based GaN production, targeting capacity availability in the second half of 2026 — a supply-chain hedge against the geopolitical risks that had unsettled the broader semiconductor industry.

By the first quarter of 2026, the first data points of recovery were visible. Revenue reached $8.6 million, up 18 percent sequentially from the declared fourth-quarter 2025 floor of $7.3 million. Gross margin expanded to 39 percent. Most significantly, the high-power segment — AI data-centre and industrial applications — grew 35 percent year-over-year and exceeded mobile revenue for the first time in the company's history. The compositional shift that Sheridan had set in motion and Allexandre had inherited was, in the language of the numbers, beginning to register.

The arc from Torrance garage to NVIDIA partner had taken eleven years and passed through two semiconductor materials, one SPAC, one acquisition, one generational CEO handoff, and one of the most dramatic single-session re-ratings in the history of the power semiconductor sector.

chapters.title: GaNFast platform, SiC portfolio, mobile-to-AI segment pivot
chapters.body:
## The Monolithic Bet: How GaNFast Works

When Gene Sheridan and Dan Kinzer incorporated Navitas in Torrance in 2014, the decisive design choice was not merely to build in gallium nitride — competitors were already doing that — but to integrate the GaN field-effect transistor, its gate driver, and its protection circuitry onto a single monolithic chip. That architectural decision, later branded GaNFast, separated Navitas from discrete-GaN rivals and became the commercial foundation on which the company was built.

The integration matters for a concrete physical reason: GaN transistors can switch at frequencies an order of magnitude higher than silicon, but realising that speed advantage requires the gate driver to sit physically close to the transistor gate. Wire-bond parasitics at gigahertz frequencies are not a rounding error but a design constraint. By embedding both the power device and its drive logic on the same die, GaNFast eliminates the parasitic inductance that would otherwise degrade switching speed and efficiency. The result is a power IC capable of switching at one to four megahertz in production designs, against fifty to two hundred kilohertz typical for silicon MOSFETs, allowing the passive components — inductors and capacitors — to shrink proportionally and enabling the compact, lightweight charger adapters that first made Navitas commercially legible to consumer OEMs.

Navitas's commercial [GaNFast catalogue](https://navitassemi.com/ganfast/) spans several voltage classes tuned to distinct power-conversion stages. The 65V and 100V families address USB Power Delivery and mobile fast-charger topologies, running AC-DC flyback converters at multi-megahertz frequencies. The 200V family extends the addressable space to laptop adapters and higher-power consumer adapters. The 650V class — the highest-voltage GaN tier in volume production at Navitas — targets AC-DC front-end stages in server power supply units, telecom rectifiers, and the grid-tied power-factor correction stages that grew in strategic importance as the company shifted its focus toward infrastructure. Each tier carries a family of SKUs differentiated by current rating and package; the 650V line in particular broadened following the NVIDIA partnership announcement of December 2024, as engineering resources were reallocated from mobile-adjacent programmes.

## GaNSafe: Engineering for the Data Centre

The GaNSafe designation, which Navitas brought to the foreground as high-power AI data centre applications moved into strategic priority, represents a hardened variant of the GaNFast platform. Where the original GaNFast focus was miniaturisation and efficiency in charger-class power levels — tens of watts to a few hundred watts — GaNSafe targets kilowatt-range power conversion in environments where a single fault carries systemic consequences.

The differentiation is primarily protective architecture. GaNSafe ICs incorporate on-chip over-current protection, gate-oxide stress monitoring, and short-circuit response circuitry that reacts within nanoseconds rather than the microseconds that external protection circuits require. At the power densities of a server rack — where a single power shelf may process ten to thirty kilowatts — the ability to self-protect without relying on a system controller prevents fault propagation before it cascades to adjacent circuitry. The GaNSafe family as commercialised spans 650V-class devices optimised for power-factor correction front ends and LLC resonant converters, the two topologies most common in enterprise power supply unit design.

## The GeneSiC Acquisition and the SiC Portfolio

Navitas closed its [acquisition of GeneSiC Semiconductor in August 2022](https://ir.navitassemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/navitas-semiconductor-completes-acquisition-genesic-semiconductor) for approximately $215 million in stock, adding a silicon carbide portfolio that extended the company's addressable market upward in voltage and outward in application. GeneSiC, founded by SiC materials specialist Ranbir Singh and headquartered in Dulles, Virginia, had built a catalogue of SiC power MOSFETs and Schottky barrier diodes spanning voltage ratings from 650V to 3,300V, with selective high-voltage offerings reaching further into the traction and industrial domains that require blocking voltages well above what any GaN device can sustain.

The strategic logic was explicit. GaN's practical ceiling in volume production sits near 650V, constrained by the substrate physics of lateral device architectures. SiC, fabricated in a vertical geometry, operates efficiently above 1,000V — the domain of motor drives, photovoltaic inverters, electric-vehicle traction inverters, and 1,500V utility-scale solar converters already consuming hundreds of millions of SiC devices per year. The acquisition gave Navitas a device for every rung of the power-conversion ladder from a USB-C charger to a grid-scale inverter.

The combined GeneSiC SiC product line as of the frozen snapshot includes standard Schottky barrier diodes, merged PiN Schottky (MPS) diodes that combine low forward voltage with elevated surge capability, and a generation of SiC MOSFETs with on-resistance figures positioned to compete with established offerings from Wolfspeed, STMicroelectronics, and Infineon across the 650V–1,700V commodity range. Navitas positioned the SiC line as a complement rather than a substitute to GaN: the two technologies serve different voltage domains and switching-frequency profiles, and a customer designing a full rack power chain might specify both within a single enclosure.

## The NVIDIA Kyber Engagement

The partnership announced on [18 December 2024](https://ir.navitassemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/navitas-semiconductor-nvidia-partner-next-generation-800v-high) between Navitas and NVIDIA provided the clearest public articulation of how Navitas's multi-technology portfolio maps onto next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA's rack-scale power programme — the Kyber architecture — specifies an 800-volt high-voltage direct-current distribution bus as the backbone for delivering power from the facility grid to the GPU compute trays. At that bus voltage the intermediate conversion losses that impair conventional 48V rack architectures diminish substantially: copper resistive losses scale with the square of current, so distributing at 800V instead of 48V reduces those losses by more than two orders of magnitude at equivalent delivered power.

Navitas's role in the Kyber power chain covers three distinct conversion stages. At the front end — the AC-DC rectifier and power-factor correction stage that converts mains alternating current to the 800V HVDC bus — GaNSafe ICs provide the switching elements, operating at 650V-class voltage ratings across the rectified AC waveform peaks. Their on-chip protection architecture is particularly valuable here, where devices switch high current at near-mains voltages and a shoot-through event would trip the entire rack's power delivery in the absence of a nanosecond-scale response.

The second stage, bus conversion from 800V HVDC down to an intermediate distribution voltage, deploys Navitas's 650V GaN ICs in LLC resonant and dual-active-bridge topologies. Both are well-matched to GaN's high switching frequency, and the conversion step from the 800V bus to a compute-shelf backplane voltage can be accomplished with peak efficiency at resonance.

The third stage is the medium-voltage secondary DC-DC conversion, where Navitas's 80–120V GaN family performs point-of-load regulation — stepping the intermediate bus voltage down to the supply rails required by individual accelerator boards and their memory subsystems. At this stage, the high switching frequency permitted by GaN allows the physical volume of conversion magnetics to shrink substantially, which matters in a GPU rack where every cubic centimetre of headroom affects the maximum thermal design power that can be sustained over sustained inference workloads.

## The Segment Pivot

For most of Navitas's post-SPAC commercial history, mobile fast-chargers defined the company's revenue profile. The USB Power Delivery boom that followed the proliferation of 65W and 100W adapters across Xiaomi, OPPO, Vivo, and OnePlus product lines gave Navitas its initial commercial scale. As recently as the quarters immediately preceding the NVIDIA announcement, mobile and consumer applications accounted for more than three-quarters of consolidated revenue — a concentration that made the company's fortunes closely correlated to Chinese consumer electronics demand cycles.

The pivot that Sheridan labelled "Navitas 2.0" involved a deliberate reallocation of engineering and commercial resources toward the high-power segment. The revenue mix shift was measurable across successive reporting periods:

| Period | Mobile / Consumer share | High-power (DC, solar, EV, industrial) share |
|---|---|---|
| FY 2023 | ~78% | ~22% |
| FY 2024 | ~55% | ~45% |
| Q4 2025 | Below 50% | Majority |

The transition carried near-term financial friction. Mobile charger revenue declined not merely as a proportion but in absolute terms as Chinese OEM design cycles matured and margin pressure from domestic GaN competitors intensified. The high-power ramp, driven by design wins carrying longer qualification cycles — particularly within the NVIDIA supply chain — did not fully offset mobile contraction in the intermediate period. Navitas addressed the liquidity dimension with a [$95.6 million private placement completed in Q4 2025](https://ir.navitassemi.com), extending cash runway to sustain engineering investment ahead of production revenue from the Kyber engagement ramping to meaningful volume.

The GaNFast platform's evolution from a mobile-charger optimisation engine to the switching core of an 800V AI data centre power train represents the most consequential technology repositioning in the company's operating history — one that Sheridan initiated and that Chris Allexandre, arriving as chief executive in September 2025, would be responsible for executing at production scale.

chapters.body:
## The arc that bent before it climbed

No number better captures Navitas Semiconductor's strategic gamble than the comparison between its 2023 revenue and its 2025 revenue: $93.0 million against $45.9 million. In most corporate narratives, a contraction of that magnitude would mark existential distress. At Navitas, management framed it as deliberate surgery — the excision of a distribution-heavy mobile fast-charger business that had inflated the revenue line while compressing the margin profile and diluting the company's identity as a power-semiconductor innovator. Whether that reframing was ultimately vindicated will depend on events still unfolding in 2026; but the financial architecture management constructed to sustain the transition — a reinforced cash position, a new manufacturing partnership, and a freshly recruited chief executive — deserves examination on its own terms.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD M) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 | $23.7 | SPAC listing year |
| 2022 | $37.9 | GeneSiC acquisition (Aug) |
| 2023 | $93.0 | Peak revenue; mobile fast-charger at scale |
| 2024 | $83.3 | Navitas 2.0 restructuring begins |
| 2025 | $45.9 | Deliberate mobile-channel exit |
| Q1 2026 | $8.6 | Sequential growth resumes |

## The growth years: 2021–2023

When Navitas completed its SPAC merger with Live Oak Acquisition Corp II on October 19, 2021, valuing the company at roughly $1 billion enterprise value, it was generating $23.7 million in annual revenue and had built its reputation almost entirely on one product concept: GaNFast, a monolithic integrated gallium nitride power IC that promised to shrink fast-charger bricks while cutting energy losses. The Chinese consumer-electronics supply chain embraced the technology early. Xiaomi, OPPO, Vivo, and OnePlus became reference customers, and their adoption pulled Navitas into a volume ramp that looked, on the revenue line, almost vertical.

By 2022 the company had added silicon carbide to its portfolio through the $215 million all-stock acquisition of GeneSiC Semiconductor in August of that year, bolting on a SiC power-device team that extended Navitas's addressable market well beyond mobile chargers toward industrial, solar, and automotive applications. Revenue climbed to $37.9 million in 2022, a year clouded by the disruption of the acquisition integration, before surging to $93.0 million in 2023 as mobile fast-charger volumes scaled and the GeneSiC SiC lines began contributing meaningfully.

At $93.0 million, Navitas appeared to have achieved escape velocity. The company was still pre-profit — it had been since founding, and the GeneSiC acquisition had added goodwill and amortisation charges that weighed on reported losses — but the revenue growth curve had become a credible argument for eventual scale economics.

## The inflection: Navitas 2.0 and the mobile exit

The 2024 figure told a different story. Revenue fell to $83.3 million, a decline management attributed partly to inventory corrections across the Chinese fast-charger supply chain and partly to the beginning of a strategic rethink. That rethink crystallised into what the company would eventually call Navitas 2.0: a deliberate withdrawal from lower-margin mobile distribution channels in favour of a concentrated push into high-power applications, principally AI data-centre infrastructure.

The strategic logic was not opaque. Mobile fast-charger revenue had been built substantially through distribution relationships in China rather than direct design-win engagements, making it susceptible to both channel inventory swings and margin pressure as GaN technology commoditised at the charger end. Meanwhile, the demand signal from AI hyperscaler infrastructure buildouts was pointing toward exactly the kind of high-voltage, high-efficiency power conversion where GaN and SiC held structural advantages over incumbent silicon.

The December 18, 2024 announcement of a strategic partnership with NVIDIA — covering next-generation 800-volt high-voltage direct-current power architecture for NVIDIA AI data-centre deployments — provided external validation for the pivot and catalysed an approximately 150 percent single-day move in Navitas's share price. The NVIDIA relationship transformed Navitas's narrative from a mobile-charger supplier in secular retreat to a designated power-semiconductor partner in the AI infrastructure stack. It also applied pressure on management to accelerate the mobile exit: maintaining the old distribution channels while pursuing mission-critical NVIDIA supply relationships would have divided engineering resources and muddied the company's customer identity.

The cost of the transition fell entirely on 2025 revenue. As Navitas systematically wound down mobile fast-charger distribution arrangements, the revenue line collapsed to $45.9 million for the full year — a contraction of roughly 45 percent from the 2024 figure and more than 50 percent from the 2023 peak.

## Finding the floor: Q4 2025

Management was explicit about where it expected the bottom to fall. The fourth quarter of 2025, stripped of the majority of the mobile distribution volume and not yet benefiting from high-power segment scale, produced revenue of $7.3 million — a figure management characterised as the trough of the Navitas 2.0 transition. That declaration of a floor was itself a form of guidance: it signalled to investors that the restructuring was not open-ended, and that the sequential recovery was expected to begin with the first quarter of 2026.

The August 31, 2025 departure of founder and chief executive Gene Sheridan — and the September 1, 2025 arrival of Chris Allexandre, who had run Renesas Electronics' power division as senior vice-president and general manager overseeing a roughly $2.5 billion revenue business — added a leadership transition to an already complex operational reset. Allexandre brought a different profile to the role: where Sheridan had been the technologist-evangelist who took Navitas from a Torrance garage to a NASDAQ listing and an NVIDIA partnership, Allexandre was a seasoned divisional executive with direct experience managing a scaled power-semiconductor business through customer qualification cycles, manufacturing negotiations, and margin discipline. Co-founder Dan Kinzer remained as chief operating officer and chief technology officer, preserving engineering continuity in the GaNFast architecture that had defined the company since 2014.

## Financial architecture: cash runway and the private placement

Management's decision to execute a $95.6 million private placement in the fourth quarter of 2025 — concurrent with the revenue trough — was structurally significant. The placement was not a distress financing; it was a runway extension timed to ensure that Navitas entered the high-power ramp with sufficient capital to sustain the lengthy qualification and volume-build cycles that AI data-centre customers impose on new suppliers.

Post-placement, Navitas carried a cash position of approximately $236.9 million. At a quarterly cash-burn rate consistent with recent operating losses, that balance represented several years of operating runway even before any material high-power revenue inflection — long enough, management argued implicitly, to reach the design-win conversion and volume ramp that the NVIDIA partnership and other AI infrastructure engagements were expected to generate.

Concurrent with the placement, Navitas disclosed a late-2025 strategic manufacturing partnership with GlobalFoundries for US-based GaN production, with targeted capacity coming online in the second half of 2026. The GlobalFoundries relationship addressed two separate investor concerns: supply-chain concentration risk (most GaN production had been routed through Asian foundries) and geopolitical exposure, as hyperscaler customers in the United States had begun to preference domestically sourced or domestically fabricated components in critical infrastructure supply chains.

## Early signs of recovery: Q1 2026

The first quarter of 2026 delivered the sequential improvement management had forecast. Revenue rose to $8.6 million, an 18 percent increase over the Q4 2025 floor. More significant than the absolute number was the compositional shift within it: the high-power segment grew 35 percent year-over-year and, for the first time in Navitas's operating history, exceeded the mobile segment in quarterly revenue contribution. Gross margin expanded to 39 percent, reflecting both the mix shift toward higher-margin high-power products and the absence of the low-margin distribution volume that had padded earlier periods.

The 39 percent gross margin remained well below the 50 percent-plus levels that mature fabless power-semiconductor businesses typically sustain, but the directional movement was consistent with the thesis that shedding mobile distribution would improve margin per dollar of revenue even as total revenue fell. Whether the margin trajectory continues toward a commercially sustainable level will depend on how quickly the high-power design wins convert to volume shipments and whether the GlobalFoundries capacity comes online on the H2 2026 schedule management communicated.

## The financial bet ahead

The Navitas 2.0 transition, viewed through a financial lens, was a wager that the margin and growth profile of the AI data-centre high-power segment would ultimately justify the revenue destruction of the mobile exit, and that the $236.9 million cash cushion was sufficient to bridge the interval between the trough and the ramp. The Q1 2026 data offered a first corroborating data point — high-power exceeding mobile, margins expanding, sequential growth resuming — but the distance between $8.6 million in quarterly revenue and the scale required to absorb Navitas's operating cost structure remained considerable.

What the financial record from 2021 through Q1 2026 ultimately described was a company that had grown fast, restructured hard, and bet its next chapter on the most capital-intensive and qualification-intensive customer segment in the power-semiconductor industry. The cash was in place, the manufacturing partnership was contracted, and the chief executive had been changed. The revenue recovery was, as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, still measured in tens of millions rather than hundreds.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## The Trough-Revenue Paradox

Navitas Semiconductor arrives at the May 2026 valuation window carrying a paradox that frustrates conventional screening but rewards scenario analysis: trailing-twelve-month revenues of approximately $42–43 million, negative EBITDA at every visible horizon, and a balance sheet holding roughly $236.9 million in unrestricted cash — a figure that, at current burn rates, finances four or more years of operations without a dollar of product revenue. Standard multiples either collapse into "not meaningful" or compress into ranges that, taken in isolation, make the stock look expensive relative to any near-term fundamental anchor. What the multiples cannot capture, and what the [December 2024 NVIDIA 800V HVDC partnership](https://ir.navitassemi.com) changed permanently, is the option value embedded in Navitas's position as the only publicly traded GaN/SiC pure-play with a named, contracted role in the power architecture of the next generation of AI data-centre infrastructure.

## Current Multiples: What the Numbers Actually Say

Management communications confirm [Q1 2026 revenue of $8.6 million](https://ir.navitassemi.com), gross margin of 39%, and 18% sequential growth from Q4 2025's declared floor of $7.3 million. Trailing-twelve-month revenue through Q1 2026 approximates $42–43 million.

Share count and market capitalisation must be estimated, and this analysis says so explicitly. Following the Q4 2025 private placement of $95.6 million and cumulative dilution from the [October 2021 SPAC merger](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001821806&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40), the August 2022 GeneSiC stock acquisition (~$215 million), and ongoing equity compensation, the fully diluted share count is estimated at approximately 210–220 million shares. The stock's price through Q1–Q2 2026 is not precisely confirmed at the frozen date; this analysis uses an implied midpoint of approximately $3.50–$4.50 per share, consistent with the post-restructuring revenue trough and the partial retracement from the December 2024 NVIDIA-announcement spike that drove approximately +150% on the day. At a $4.00 midpoint and 215 million diluted shares, market capitalisation approximates $860 million. Net enterprise value, backing out the $236.9 million cash position, sits at roughly $630–650 million.

The resulting EV/TTM Sales multiple is approximately **15x**. Forward EV/Sales, applying a conservative 2026 full-year revenue estimate of $55–65 million reflecting management's H2 2026 acceleration thesis and GlobalFoundries US-based GaN capacity coming online, compresses to roughly **10–11x**. Price-to-earnings and EV/EBITDA remain not meaningful — the company runs at an operating loss and is managed explicitly for strategic positioning over near-term profitability. Price-to-book, applying the $236.9 million cash position as a hard floor, implies approximately 3.6x book value at the midpoint market cap estimate, meaning the market pays a roughly 2.6x premium over net tangible assets for the strategic option value.

## Historical Multiple Context: Re-Rating and Partial Retracement

The stock's post-SPAC multiple history falls into three distinct regimes. From the October 2021 listing through mid-2023, Navitas traded at EV/forward-Sales multiples of 8–20x on mobile fast-charger revenue ramp enthusiasm, briefly touching 25x at the SPAC-premium peak. The 2023–2024 compression phase, driven by mobile segment deceleration and the strategic pivot toward high-power AI data-centre customers, brought the multiple down sharply — EV/Sales troughed near 5–7x through mid-2024 as [revenue retreated from its $93 million 2023 peak](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001821806&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40) toward $83.3 million in 2024 and then $45.9 million in 2025 under the deliberate Navitas 2.0 channel restructuring.

The December 2024 NVIDIA partnership announcement was the single largest re-rating event in the company's public history. A named, strategic relationship with the world's leading AI accelerator company — specifically tied to 800V HVDC power architecture underpinning the next-generation data-centre build — repriced Navitas from a struggling mobile-chip transitional story to a pure-play AI infrastructure input. The multiple expanded sharply before partially retracing as 2025 revenue compression materialised. By the frozen-snapshot window, the stock trades at a meaningful premium to its 2024 trough multiples but well below the NVIDIA-announcement spike, representing a partial de-rating that has not fully unwound the strategic premium.

## Peer-Group Comparison

The absence of a direct public-market peer — a GaN/SiC pure-play at comparable scale — forces comparison across overlapping sets: other wide-bandgap power semiconductor players, and high-growth power-management IC companies with AI data-centre exposure.

| Company | Ticker | Approx. Mkt Cap | EV/NTM Sales | EV/NTM EBITDA | NTM Rev. Growth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Navitas Semiconductor** | **NVTS** | **~$860M** | **~10–11x** | **NM** | **~+30–40% (est.)** |
| Wolfspeed | WOLF | ~$700M | ~3x | NM | Declining |
| Monolithic Power Systems | MPWR | ~$17B | ~11x | ~28x | ~+15% |
| Power Integrations | POWI | ~$2.5B | ~4x | ~15x | ~+5% |
| onsemi | ON | ~$12B | ~2.5x | ~8x | ~–5% |
| MACOM Technology Solutions | MTSI | ~$6B | ~9x | ~22x | ~+15% |

*All peer multiples approximate as of late May 2026. NM = not meaningful.*

The table illustrates a bifurcation. Wolfspeed — the closest structural analog as a WBG pure-play — trades at a steep discount to Navitas on EV/Sales, reflecting Wolfspeed's deeper operational distress and balance-sheet pressure versus Navitas's newly reinforced cash position. Monolithic Power Systems and MACOM, the premium-multiple AI-infrastructure-adjacent power-IC names, trade at comparable EV/Sales but carry positive EBITDA, grounding their multiples in actual earnings power. Navitas's premium over distressed peers and near-parity with profitable ones is defensible only so long as the NVIDIA partnership converts to demonstrable revenue at scale within the next two to three years.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Current Price Implies

A simplified reverse-DCF reveals the implied cash-flow trajectory the $630–650 million net EV demands. Assuming a 15% cost of capital, a terminal EV/EBITDA exit multiple of 18x, and reaching EBITDA break-even by 2028, the current net EV implies peak-cycle revenue in the $250–300 million range by 2029–2030. That scenario requires Navitas to compound revenue at approximately 50–60% per annum from the 2026 trough — achievable only if the NVIDIA 800V HVDC ramp delivers the volume pull-through management has indicated and the GlobalFoundries US manufacturing partnership removes the supply constraint that capped prior growth cycles.

The cash backstop is meaningful in this framework. The $236.9 million cash position — approximately 27 cents of cash per dollar of market capitalisation at the midpoint estimate — caps the downside scenario. Even under severe bear assumptions, the company faces no near-term solvency risk, and the cash burns slowly enough to allow multiple NVIDIA programme qualification cycles.

## Bull / Base / Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $8.00–$10.00 implied price:** The NVIDIA 800V HVDC partnership moves from qualification to production-volume pull in H2 2026 as next-generation data-centre build-out accelerates. GlobalFoundries US-based GaN capacity enables domestic content eligibility. 2027 revenue reaches $180–220 million at 45% gross margins, approaching EBITDA break-even. EV/2027 Sales re-rates to 12–14x on profitability visibility. The GeneSiC SiC portfolio wins incremental electric-vehicle traction adoption in parallel. Probability assigned: approximately 25%.

**Base case — $4.00–$5.50 implied price:** The NVIDIA partnership ramps but more gradually, with programme qualification extending into mid-2027. 2026 revenue reaches $55–65 million. Gross margins expand toward 42–44%. The company remains EBITDA-negative through 2027 but demonstrates a credible trajectory. EV/2027 Sales compresses modestly as the street gains confidence in the ramp. Mobile generates residual cash flow to partially fund operations. Probability assigned: approximately 50%.

**Bear case — $1.50–$2.50 implied price:** The NVIDIA partnership produces qualification volumes but not commercial-scale pull, delayed by competing architectures or NVIDIA internal supply-chain decisions. Revenue remains in the $40–55 million range through 2027. Cash burns toward $150 million. A follow-on equity raise at distressed prices dilutes existing holders materially. The stock gravitates toward a 5–6x EV/Sales multiple on flat or declining growth, partially offset by the cash floor. Probability assigned: approximately 25%.

## What the Market Is Pricing In — and the Gap

Consensus estimates, reconstructed from available buy-side commentary through the frozen window, appear to embed a scenario close to the base case but with a modestly more optimistic 2026 revenue assumption of $65–75 million — perhaps one to two quarters ahead of what the $8.6 million Q1 2026 data point straightforwardly supports. The gap between consensus and this dossier's read is not directional but temporal. The dossier assigns higher probability to a 2027 rather than 2026 inflection in meaningful NVIDIA volumes, and correspondingly higher weight to the bear-case tail than consensus appears to embed.

What the market does not fully price, and what this chapter flags as the asymmetric upside, is the regulatory and geopolitical dimension: a US-manufactured GaN supply chain, delivered through the GlobalFoundries partnership, in a policy environment actively incentivising domestic semiconductor capacity. If that supply positioning earns Navitas a preferred-supplier designation within NVIDIA's data-centre vendor programmes — bypassing competitive procurement processes that would otherwise compress margin — the bull-case multiples become substantially more defensible. That premium is not yet in the price.

chapters.title: Post-SPAC quarters through NVIDIA partnership and Allexandre era
chapters.body:
## From Nasdaq Debut to the First Test of Scale

Navitas Semiconductor completed its merger with Live Oak Acquisition Corp II in October 2021, pegging enterprise value at approximately $1 billion — a rich multiple for a company that had recorded just $23.7 million in full-year revenue. The transaction placed Gene Sheridan's GaN pure-play alongside a cohort of power-semiconductor newcomers chasing the electrification wave, but it also handed him a public-company clock, an expectant investor base, and the obligation to prove that gallium nitride could graduate from smartphone chargers to the industrial and automotive volumes that justify billion-dollar valuations. [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001821806](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001821806)

The first post-SPAC fiscal year delivered an encouraging answer. Revenue rose to $37.9 million in 2022, a 60% advance on the prior year, propelled by accelerating design wins in mobile fast charging as GaNFast-enabled adapters were qualified and shipped by an expanding roster of consumer-electronics original equipment manufacturers across Asia. Then, in August 2022, Navitas folded in GeneSiC Semiconductor — a Dulles, Virginia-based silicon carbide specialist founded by Ranbir Singh — broadening its portfolio beyond GaN into the SiC devices that EV powertrain and industrial power conversion demanded. The acquisition completed the compound-semiconductor stack Sheridan had articulated since the company's 2014 Torrance founding: wide-bandgap SiC for high-voltage, high-temperature applications; GaN for the fast-switching, high-efficiency charger and adapter markets.

## The 2023 Peak and the Pivot Decision

Fiscal 2023 was the top of the first arc. Revenue reached $93.0 million — more than doubling the prior-year figure — as mobile fast-charger volumes swelled and the GeneSiC SiC lines contributed their first full year of post-acquisition revenue. The growth validated the land-and-expand logic of the dual-technology strategy. Yet the composition of those revenues carried a structural tension: a disproportionate share originated in lower-margin distribution channels serving the Asian consumer-electronics supply chain, channels that offered volume but not the system-level design relationships or application content that Navitas had built its equity story upon.

The 2024 fiscal year surfaced that tension. Revenue contracted to $83.3 million as mobile charger demand cooled and Navitas began deliberate work exiting lower-margin channels. Gross margin pressure followed. The strategic question was whether to defend revenue at the cost of mix, or absorb a near-term topline haircut in exchange for repositioning the company toward high-power, high-content segments — data-centre infrastructure, EV on-board charging, solar inverters — where wide-bandgap semiconductors command meaningfully better economics.

## The NVIDIA Partnership and the Re-rating

The December 2024 announcement of a strategic partnership with NVIDIA for 800-volt high-voltage direct-current data-centre power architecture resolved that question with unusual clarity. [Navitas IR](https://ir.navitassemi.com) The partnership aligned Navitas GaN and SiC technology with NVIDIA's next-generation GPU rack infrastructure, which required power conversion at voltages and switching frequencies that conventional silicon IGBTs cannot efficiently achieve. For a company whose entire founding thesis had been predicated on the superior switching efficiency of wide-bandgap materials at high frequency, the NVIDIA relationship was simultaneously commercial validation and the single largest re-rating event in the company's post-SPAC history.

The structural logic was compelling. An 800-volt HVDC data-centre power shelf consumed more GaN content than hundreds of consumer adapters. The partnership positioned Navitas to participate in that content expansion with a tier-one AI hardware customer as design-win anchor, at a moment when hyperscaler capital expenditure on AI infrastructure was accelerating across every major market.

## Navitas 2.0: The Revenue Floor and the Recapitalisation

The strategic pivot carried a near-term cost that management named without equivocation. The deliberate exit from lower-margin mobile distribution channels compressed full-year 2025 revenue to $45.9 million — a 45% decline from the 2023 peak — as Navitas shed the volume that had inflated its topline without commensurate margin or strategic content. Management designated the programme "Navitas 2.0," framing it as the transition from a GaN-and-SiC components supplier to a high-power platform company serving AI data-centre and EV infrastructure.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD) | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 | $23.7M | Pre-SPAC GaNFast mobile ramp |
| 2022 | $37.9M | Post-SPAC scale; GeneSiC acquired Aug 2022 |
| 2023 | $93.0M | Peak; mobile volume + first full GeneSiC year |
| 2024 | $83.3M | Channel exits begin; mix pressure |
| 2025 | $45.9M | Navitas 2.0 restructuring; mobile shed |
| Q1 2026 | $8.6M | First Allexandre quarter; high-power crossover |

The fourth quarter of 2025, at $7.3 million in revenue, was what management characterised as the trough. To fund the transition through to the anticipated high-power revenue ramp, Navitas executed a $95.6 million private placement in the quarter, leaving the company with approximately $236.9 million in cash — a runway engineered to bridge the gap between the mobile-exit trough and data-centre volume shipments. In parallel, a late-2025 strategic partnership with GlobalFoundries established US-based GaN production capacity targeting availability in the second half of 2026, a supply-chain hedge against geopolitical concentration risk and a potential differentiator for US-domiciled data-centre customers with domestic-sourcing requirements.

## The Sheridan-to-Allexandre Succession

On August 31, 2025, Gene Sheridan stepped down as chief executive after eleven years leading the company he had co-founded with Dan Kinzer. The transition was framed as orderly and planned; Kinzer remained as co-founder, chief operating officer, and chief technology officer, preserving the engineering continuity that had produced GaNFast and the underlying GaN platform intellectual property. The board named Chris Allexandre as chief executive effective September 1, 2025.

Allexandre arrived with credentials calibrated to Navitas's new strategic posture. He had served as senior vice president and general manager of Renesas Electronics' Power Division — a business running approximately $2.5 billion in revenue — bringing the large-scale semiconductor operating experience that the transition from founder-led start-up to industrial-scale power platform demanded. Where Sheridan's profile was that of a founder who had evangelised wide-bandgap technology through its early-adoption phase, Allexandre's was that of an operator who had managed a business already at the scale Navitas was targeting.

## Q1 2026: The First Allexandre Quarter

The first earnings report under Allexandre's stewardship, covering the quarter ended March 2026, offered early evidence that the trough management had called in Q4 2025 was holding. [Navitas IR](https://ir.navitassemi.com) Revenue of $8.6 million represented an 18% sequential improvement over Q4 2025's floor.

The high-power segment — encompassing data-centre, EV, and industrial applications — grew 35% year-over-year and surpassed mobile revenue for the first time, a crossover that management had projected as the structural proof point of the Navitas 2.0 repositioning. Gross margin expanded to 39%, reflecting the improved mix quality that the deliberate channel exits had been designed to produce. The GlobalFoundries capacity build was tracking toward a second-half 2026 availability, providing the manufacturing infrastructure necessary to support data-centre customer qualifications at volume.

The Q1 2026 results did not erase two years of revenue compression, nor did they signal that data-centre shipments had reached meaningful scale. What they established was that the mix transition was executing to plan, that the cost structure had been reset to the lower revenue base, and that the NVIDIA partnership and the domestic capacity build were advancing toward the second-half 2026 inflection both Allexandre's team and the board had telegraphed. For a company that spent a decade building the technology and a further two years rebuilding the business model around it, Q1 2026 was the first quarter that looked more like an opening than a turn.

chapters.title: Sheridan, Allexandre, Kinzer, and the post-SPAC board
chapters.body:
## From International Rectifier to Pure-Play Pioneer

When Gene Sheridan and Dan Kinzer left International Rectifier in 2014 to found Navitas Semiconductor in Torrance, California, they brought with them something as commercially durable as any patent: the institutional knowledge of a company that had defined discrete power semiconductors for a generation. International Rectifier, founded in 1947 and acquired by Infineon Technologies in a $3 billion transaction completed in January 2015, had spent decades building the technical and commercial infrastructure of silicon-based power conversion. Sheridan had risen to Senior Vice President of Worldwide Sales and Marketing — a role that gave him global customer relationships, channel architecture experience, and the commercial instincts that would anchor Navitas's go-to-market strategy. Kinzer had spent a parallel career on the engineering side, accumulating the materials science and circuit design depth that commercializing gallium nitride at scale would demand.

Their timing reflected a clear-eyed read of where the power semiconductor industry was heading. GaN's theoretical advantages over silicon — higher switching frequency, lower switching losses, smaller form factor — had been understood in research circles for years. What was missing was a dedicated commercial organization willing to build GaN power ICs from scratch without the legacy silicon product lines that complicated investment decisions at incumbents. Navitas was founded as precisely that vehicle: a pure-play with no silicon revenue to protect and no internal constituency arguing against cannibalizing the old technology.

Sheridan held the title of Co-founder, President, and Chief Executive Officer continuously from the company's founding through August 31, 2025 — a run of eleven years that encompassed the full arc from pre-revenue startup to SPAC-listed public company to NVIDIA strategic partner. His undergraduate degree in electrical engineering from the University of California, San Diego, placed him in a generation of IR executives who had come up through the engineering side before moving into commercial roles, a combination that proved particularly suited to selling nascent semiconductor technology into conservative industrial and consumer OEM purchasing organizations that required technical credibility alongside commercial relationships.

## The Engineering Anchor: Dan Kinzer and GaNFast

If Sheridan provided the commercial and strategic axis around which Navitas oriented, Kinzer provided the technical one. As co-founder, Chief Operating Officer, and Chief Technology Officer — a combined role that reflected both the company's scale and Kinzer's range — he oversaw the development of the GaNFast platform, Navitas's flagship monolithic integrated GaN power IC architecture. The core insight behind GaNFast was the integration of gate driver, protection, and logic functions onto a single GaN-on-silicon die, a departure from the discrete GaN transistors offered by earlier-generation competitors and a significant reduction in the bill-of-materials complexity that had historically constrained GaN adoption outside premium consumer and industrial applications.

Kinzer's continuous tenure through the October 2021 SPAC listing, the August 2022 GeneSiC acquisition, and the December 2024 NVIDIA 800V partnership announcement represented a form of technical institutional memory that Navitas's board consistently treated as a core retention priority. When the company's product portfolio extended from GaN into silicon carbide through the GeneSiC acquisition — adding Ranbir Singh, GeneSiC's founder and the principal architect of its SiC power device portfolio, to the engineering leadership — Kinzer's COO/CTO mandate expanded to encompass the integration of two fundamentally different wide-bandgap device families under a single operational structure. That he did so without a significant post-acquisition engineering departure represented a meaningful execution result in a sector where acquired technical talent regularly exits within eighteen months of deal close.

## The Financial Architecture: Todd Glickman

Todd Glickman's tenure as Chief Financial Officer spanned the full transformation of Navitas from private entity to public company to would-be AI infrastructure supplier. He was in place for the October 2021 merger with Live Oak Acquisition Corp II at approximately $1 billion enterprise value; he structured the financing of the $215 million all-stock acquisition of GeneSiC Semiconductor in August 2022; and he managed the capital structure through the Q4 2025 private placement that raised $95.6 million, extending the company's runway as the Navitas 2.0 pivot toward AI data center infrastructure consumed engineering and commercial resources in advance of revenue conversion.

The continuity of CFO function across those structurally distinct transactions — a SPAC merger, an all-stock acquisition, and a dilutive private placement — was not incidental. Capital markets credibility at a loss-making pure-play accumulates slowly and depletes quickly; Glickman's ability to return to the same institutional investors across successive financing events reflected a relationship asset that is difficult to rebuild after a CFO transition. The board's retention of Glickman through the 2025 CEO succession, even as the operating leadership changed, was a deliberate governance choice.

## The Succession: Chris Allexandre

The transition that the Navitas board had been engineering for at least a year arrived formally on September 1, 2025, when Chris Allexandre succeeded Sheridan as Chief Executive Officer. Sheridan remained on the board, and the company described the move in the language of planned succession — an organization that had concluded the skills required to grow a product from commercial launch to mobile fast-charger market leadership were different from those required to win AI data center procurement decisions at hyperscale and manage the operational complexity of a company scaling toward profitability.

Allexandre came from Renesas Electronics, where he had run the Power Division as Senior Vice President and General Manager — a business generating approximately $2.5 billion in annual revenue. The contrast in operating scale was deliberate. Navitas's opportunity, particularly in the context of the NVIDIA partnership and the 800V high-voltage direct-current architecture for AI data center power distribution, was not a business that would be won by a management team calibrated to its current revenue base. The board was hiring for the company Navitas intended to become.

Allexandre's Renesas background also brought supply chain and manufacturing relationships germane to Navitas's scaling challenge. The company had historically operated a fabless model, relying on external foundries for GaN-on-silicon production — a structure that kept capital requirements manageable in the early growth phase but created capacity and lead-time exposure as revenue scaled. The GlobalFoundries manufacturing partnership announced in late 2025, establishing US-based GaN production capacity targeted at H2 2026 readiness, represented precisely the supply chain architecture decision that a CEO with Allexandre's manufacturing-scale experience was positioned to execute. Sheridan's transition to a board director role rather than a full exit was equally significant: his NVIDIA partner relationships and product roadmap knowledge were not transferable on a ninety-day handover schedule, and the board structured the succession accordingly.

## The Board: SPAC Heritage and Strategic Additions

Navitas's eight-member board in the post-succession period reflected the layered history of a company that came public through a SPAC, made a material acquisition in its first year as a listed entity, and then pivoted its primary application market within three years of listing. The composition paired the co-founder executives with an independent director set assembled across three distinct periods.

Brian Long, the Independent Board Chair, brought the governance weight of a seasoned technology-industry executive and investor. His chairmanship through the 2024–2025 strategic inflection — the NVIDIA partnership announcement, the Allexandre hire, and the Q4 2025 capital raise — provided the oversight continuity that public-company governance requires when executive leadership is simultaneously in transition and under the most acute commercial scrutiny in the company's history.

Richard Hendrix represented the most direct institutional link to the SPAC formation. As a principal associated with Live Oak Acquisition Corp II — the blank-check vehicle that combined with Navitas in October 2021 — Hendrix's continuing board presence preserved the transaction memory that underpins the company's public capital structure. The retention of SPAC-associated directors into the post-merger period is not standard practice; Navitas's choice reflected a board composition philosophy that valued deal continuity alongside operational independence.

The four remaining independent directors brought complementary governance profiles across finance, technology operations, and audit oversight:

| Director | Role | Principal Governance Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| Brian Long | Independent Chair | Technology executive and investor; governance continuity through strategic inflection |
| Gene Sheridan | Executive Director | Co-founder; post-succession advisory continuity; NVIDIA partner relationship |
| Dan Kinzer | Executive Director | Co-founder; GaNFast and SiC engineering continuity |
| Richard Hendrix | Independent Director | Live Oak Acquisition Corp II / SPAC transaction institutional memory |
| Garry Mexted | Independent Director | Corporate finance and public-company governance |
| David Moxam | Independent Director | Technology-industry operating experience |
| Cristiano Amoruso | Independent Director | Technology-industry executive and strategic oversight |
| Susan Pickering | Independent Director | Finance governance; audit committee depth |

Mexted's corporate finance background carried particular relevance through the 2025 capital events. Moxam and Amoruso provided the technology-industry operating context relevant to evaluating the strategic bets embedded in the Navitas 2.0 pivot. Pickering's finance governance profile completed the audit and compensation committee infrastructure that SEC reporting obligations require of a NASDAQ-listed small-cap.

## Governance in Transition

The twelve months following Allexandre's appointment constituted the most complex governance period in Navitas's public history. The NVIDIA partnership demanded executive bandwidth on partner management and commercial roadmap alignment at the same moment the company was managing a CEO handover. The GlobalFoundries agreement required capital commitment decisions with multi-year supply chain consequences. The Q4 2025 private placement involved dilution negotiations at a stock price that had appreciated approximately 150 percent on the December 2024 NVIDIA announcement before a subsequent revaluation as the market assessed the distance between partnership announcement and revenue recognition.

The governance triangle that Long, Sheridan, and Allexandre occupied — independent chair, outgoing founder on the board, incoming operating CEO — was designed to transfer institutional knowledge without diluting the new chief executive's operational authority. Kinzer's position as the remaining co-founder in an active operating role anchored the platform's technical credibility through the succession. In a company whose entire value proposition rests on engineering differentiation in a materials science still commercially maturing, CTO continuity mattered as much to customer confidence as any financial disclosure. The board's preservation of both co-founders in active roles — one operational, one advisory — was its most legible statement that the succession from Sheridan to Allexandre was a commercial and strategic transition, not an engineering one.

chapters.title: NVIDIA, mobile OEMs, foundry partnerships, and HALEU-style scarcity of GaN capacity
chapters.body:
## The Partnership That Rewired the Thesis

On the morning of December 18, 2024, Navitas Semiconductor's share price roughly doubled — and then kept climbing. By the close of trading, the stock had surged approximately 150 percent on a single press release: a [strategic partnership with NVIDIA](https://ir.navitassemi.com) to supply power-conversion silicon for the next generation of 800V high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) data-centre infrastructure. The architecture in question was NVIDIA's Kyber rack-scale platform, the dense compute chassis designed to run Rubin Ultra GPUs at power densities that conventional 48V DC power delivery could not economically support.

The announcement was, in the most literal sense, a re-rating event. For four years after its October 2021 SPAC listing, Navitas had traded primarily as a mobile-charger play — a pure-play GaN semiconductor company that had ridden the global rollout of USB Power Delivery fast-chargers into the smartphones of hundreds of millions of consumers. The NVIDIA press release compressed that identity into a footnote. In a single trading session, the market assigned Navitas a new narrative: AI infrastructure power.

The underlying technical logic was straightforward. At 800V HVDC, the conversion losses and copper costs that make conventional data-centre power delivery prohibitive can be dramatically reduced. A 10-megawatt rack cluster running on 800V HVDC requires roughly one-third the copper weight of an equivalent 48V DC installation, and the switching frequency at which GaN power ICs operate — ten to one-hundred times faster than legacy silicon MOSFETs — allows the passive components (inductors, capacitors) to shrink proportionally. For rack-scale AI compute, where power density is a first-order constraint on how many GPUs can be packed into a floor tile, those efficiency and density gains are not incremental. They are architectural.

## A Legacy Business Deliberately Dismantled

To understand what Navitas was selling before NVIDIA called, it is necessary to account for the customer base it was simultaneously walking away from. Through 2022 and into 2023, the company's revenues were anchored in mobile fast-charger OEMs — Xiaomi, OPPO, Vivo, OnePlus — whose adoption of GaNFast power ICs had driven annual revenues from $23.7 million in 2021 to $93.0 million in 2023. GaNFast's monolithic integration of gate driver and GaN transistor on a single die gave these OEM customers a charger brick that was smaller, lighter, and ran cooler than the equivalent silicon solution. In the hyper-competitive Chinese smartphone accessories market, that differentiation translated into shelf placement and margin.

The problem, as management diagnosed it under the Navitas 2.0 restructuring banner, was structural. Mobile fast-charger volumes are inherently lumpy, tied to handset upgrade cycles and platform transitions. Gross margins in the distribution-heavy channels serving Chinese OEMs were thin. And as GaN charger penetration matured — moving from premium to mid-range handsets — the technology was commoditising faster than Navitas's product roadmap could sustain a premium. Revenue that had peaked at $93.0 million in 2023 contracted to $83.3 million in 2024 and then fell sharply to approximately $45.9 million in 2025 as the company deliberately shed lower-margin distribution revenue and accepted the near-term pain.

The strategic logic was explicit in management's framing: Navitas 2.0 was a triage operation, not a crisis. The company was choosing to compress the top line in order to reposition the customer mix toward high-power AI data centre accounts where average selling prices, design-win durability, and gross margin profiles are categorically different from consumer electronics. The inflection point arrived in Q1 2026, when the high-power segment — AI data centre and industrial — exceeded mobile revenue for the first time in the company's history, with high-power growing 35 percent year-over-year against a mobile segment that continued to shrink.

## The Foundry Map: TSMC, GlobalFoundries, and Domestic Capacity

Navitas operates as a fabless designer. Its GaNFast monolithic ICs — and the GaN-on-silicon process that makes them manufacturable at commercial scale — depend entirely on foundry partners willing and able to run the compound-semiconductor processes that silicon-only fabs cannot accommodate. That dependency has historically pointed to a small number of foundries globally with GaN-on-silicon capability at production volume.

The late-2025 announcement of a strategic manufacturing partnership with GlobalFoundries was the most significant supply-chain event of the NVIDIA partnership era for reasons that extended beyond mere capacity addition. GlobalFoundries operates fabs in Malta, New York and Burlington, Vermont — domestic US production sites eligible for CHIPS and Science Act incentive programmes and insulated from the export-control and geopolitical risk that attaches to Taiwan-centric supply chains at a moment when AI infrastructure is a declared national-security priority in Washington. The GlobalFoundries partnership targets H2 2026 for initial GaN production capacity — a timeline that aligns, non-coincidentally, with the ramp cycles for NVIDIA's Kyber rack deployments.

The TSMC relationship, which underpinned earlier GaNFast generations, represented the incumbent foundry axis. TSMC's compound-semiconductor speciality processes have provided Navitas with production-grade GaN-on-silicon capability and the process stability required for consumer electronics qualification. However, TSMC's Taiwan concentration carries supply-chain concentration risk that enterprise data-centre customers — and their procurement executives at hyperscalers under pressure from regulators and boards — have become sensitised to in the post-pandemic, post-Ukraine era. The GlobalFoundries partnership is, among other things, a geographic diversification of that risk.

The combined foundry posture — TSMC as incumbent, GlobalFoundries as the US-domiciled scale-up vehicle — mirrors the dual-source strategies that Navitas's own OEM customers have demanded from their suppliers for decades. Applied to the company's own supply chain, it is a posture shift that reflects the institutional expectations of AI infrastructure customers, who are not smartphone accessory buyers and will not accept single-source concentration at a component tier this critical.

## The GaN Capacity Problem: A HALEU-Style Constraint

There is a parallel between the scarcity dynamics governing GaN power-IC production capacity and those that have historically constrained HALEU — high-assay low-enriched uranium — for advanced nuclear reactors. In both cases, the underlying technology requires a specialised physical plant that decades of commercial incentive have not produced in abundance, and the installed base of capable production infrastructure is a small fraction of what an accelerating demand curve could absorb.

GaN-on-silicon is not a substrate-scarce technology in the way that silicon carbide is. SiC wafers — critical to the GeneSiC product lines Navitas absorbed in its August 2022 acquisition — have faced documented supply constraints, with Wolfspeed's wafer output a binding variable on industry-wide SiC device availability. GaN-on-silicon, by contrast, grows on standard silicon substrates. The constraint is process capability: the epitaxial deposition steps, the device isolation architectures, and the metallisation schemes required to produce GaN-on-silicon reliably at high yield are non-trivial, and the number of foundries globally that can run them at production scale is narrow.

That narrowness acquires strategic weight as AI infrastructure spending scales. NVIDIA's Kyber deployment roadmap, if it proceeds on the timelines implied by Rubin Ultra GPU availability, will require GaN power conversion silicon in volumes that the existing qualified supply base will struggle to satisfy without deliberate capacity investment. GlobalFoundries' commitment to H2 2026 GaN capacity is a response to that anticipated scarcity — an attempt, in effect, to add enrichment capacity before the fuel demand arrives rather than after.

The packaging dimension compounds the constraint. GaN power ICs at the voltages and switching frequencies required for 800V HVDC applications place thermal and parasitic-inductance demands on package design that conventional MOSFET packaging cannot meet. Advanced packaging — direct-bonded copper substrates, kelvin-source connections, low-inductance land-grid-array formats — requires packaging supply-chain partners with their own specialised tooling. Navitas has developed packaging intellectual property alongside its GaNFast IC design, but the packaging ecosystem remains a secondary bottleneck that the broader GaN industry has been slower to address than the wafer-level process.

## SiC: The GeneSiC Overhang

The GeneSiC acquisition brought Navitas a SiC Schottky diode and MOSFET portfolio designed primarily for industrial, solar, and EV applications. The SiC wafer supply situation — endemic across the industry — has pressured margins and delivery timelines for products that depend on large-diameter SiC substrates. Wolfspeed's capacity expansion at its Mohawk Valley fab, and the broader industry push toward 200mm SiC wafers, represents the medium-term resolution path, but the timeline is measured in years rather than quarters.

For Navitas, the SiC portfolio's near-term contribution to the AI data-centre thesis is secondary to GaN; the high-power AI segment growth that drove Q1 2026 outperformance was GaN-centric.
